Appointment
ap-point'-ment
n. (an ordering or direction; in the Authorized Version, chiefly the word of a man by which a matter is settled)
From appoint, Old French apointier, to arrange or settle. The Hebrew idiom behind three of the occurrences is literally at the mouth of — a thing done at the mouth of Aaron, at the mouth of Absalom — so that an appointment in Scripture is a spoken order that stands.

Biblical Definition

The Hebrew phrase rendered appointment is literally at the mouth of, and the four occurrences show what a mouth can order. Holy service: “At the appointment of Aaron and his sons shall be all the service of the sons of the Gershonites, in all their burdens” (Num 4:27) — even the carrying of curtains was not left to preference; the sanctuary was borne according to a word. Provision for worship: the Persian king decrees that bullocks, rams, lambs, wheat, salt, wine and oil be given “according to the appointment of the priests which are at Jerusalem… day by day without fail” (Ezr 6:9) — a pagan emperor funding the temple at the priests' direction, which is the LORD turning the king's heart whithersoever He will. Murder: “by the appointment of Absalom this hath been determined from the day that he forced his sister Tamar” (2Sa 13:32) — two years of silence, and the whole time a word had been spoken and stood. And friendship: Job's three friends “had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him” (Job 2:11), and they kept it, and sat seven days without speaking, which was the best thing they ever did. Service, provision, murder, and comfort: all settled by an appointment, all standing on somebody's word.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines appointment as the act of appointing, designation to office; stipulation, agreement; and decree, established order or constitution.

expand to see more

APPOINTMENT, n. The act of appointing; designation to office; as, he erred by the appointment of unsuitable men.

1. Stipulation; agreement; the act of fixing by mutual agreement; as, they made an appointment to meet at six.

2. Decree; established order or constitution; as, it is our duty to submit to the divine appointments.

3. Direction; order; command.

Key Scripture

Num 4:27 — "At the appointment of Aaron and his sons shall be all the service of the sons of the Gershonites, in all their burdens, and in all their service: and ye shall appoint unto them in charge all their burdens."

Job 2:11 — "Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him."

2Sa 13:32 — "And Jonadab, the son of Shimeah David's brother, answered and said, Let not my lord suppose that they have slain all the young men the king's sons; for Amnon only is dead: for by the appointment of Absalom this hath been determined from the day that he forced his sister Tamar."

Ezr 6:9 — "And that which they have need of, both young bullocks, and rams, and lambs, for the burnt offerings of the God of heaven, wheat, salt, wine, and oil, according to the appointment of the priests which are at Jerusalem, let it be given them day by day without fail:"

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word means today roughly what it meant in 1611 — an arrangement fixed by a word — though the modern ear hears mainly the calendar sense and misses the older sense of authoritative direction that governs Numbers 4:27 and Ezra 6:9.

The principle to recover is that the service of God is ordered rather than improvised. The Gershonites did not choose which burdens to carry; the appointment came from the priesthood, and the burdens were assigned by name. That instinct stands behind the regulative principle of worship: God is served according to His word and not according to the taste of the servants, and the freedom of a worshipper lies in knowing exactly what he has been given to carry. Job's friends give the pastoral form of the same thing — they made an appointment to come, and they came. Comfort in Scripture is rarely spontaneous; it is usually the keeping of a resolution to show up.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew peh (H6310), mouth — the idiom at the mouth of, rendered appointment; ya'ad (H3259), to appoint, to meet by agreement; ta'am (H2942), decree.

expand to see more

Hebrew peh (H6310) — mouth; the literal idiom in Numbers 4:27 and 2 Samuel 13:32, at the mouth of Aaron, of Absalom — an order that stands because it was spoken by one with authority.

Hebrew ya'ad (H3259) — to appoint, to fix a time, to meet by agreement; Job 2:11, of the three friends.

Hebrew ta'am (H2942) — decree, command; Ezra 6:9, the Persian decree for the temple's supply.

Hebrew mo'ed (H4150) — an appointed time or meeting; the root of the tabernacle of the congregation, the tent of meeting.

Greek tasso (G5021) — to arrange, appoint, ordain; Acts 13:48, as many as were ordained to eternal life believed.

Usage

"“At the appointment of Aaron and his sons” — even the curtains were carried by order."

"“They had made an appointment together… to comfort him” — and they came."

"“By the appointment of Absalom” — two silent years, and a word standing the whole time."
